subject: physics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What is the SI unit of electric current?
questions.explain: Electric current is measured in amperes (A), where one ampere is a flow of one coulomb per second.

questions.q: Which equation correctly relates charge Q, current I and time t?
questions.explain: Charge equals current multiplied by time, so Q = It, measured in coulombs.

questions.q: A current of 2 A flows through a wire for 30 s. How much charge passes a point in the wire?
questions.explain: Using Q = It = 2 A x 30 s = 60 C.

questions.q: Two lamps are connected in series. What is true about the current through them?
options: The current is the same through both lamps
The current is largest in the first lamp
The current splits equally between the lamps
The current is zero in the second lamp
questions.explain: In a series circuit the current is the same at every point because there is only one path for charge to flow.

questions.q: Which equation defines the resistance of a component?
questions.explain: Potential difference equals current multiplied by resistance, V = IR.

questions.q: A current of 4 A flows through a 5 ohm resistor. What is the potential difference across it?
questions.explain: Using V = IR = 4 A x 5 ohm = 20 V.

questions.q: Two resistors are connected in parallel across a battery. What is true about the potential difference across them?
options: The potential difference is the same across each resistor
The potential difference is shared between them
The potential difference is largest across the smaller resistor
The potential difference is zero across both
questions.explain: Components connected in parallel have the same potential difference across each branch.

questions.q: What is the potential difference (voltage) of the UK domestic mains supply?
questions.explain: The UK mains supply has a nominal potential difference of 230 V.

questions.q: What is the frequency of the UK alternating mains supply?
questions.explain: The UK mains is an alternating current with a frequency of 50 Hz.

questions.q: In a UK three-pin plug, what colour is the insulation on the live wire?
questions.explain: The live wire is brown, the neutral is blue and the earth is green and yellow.

questions.q: What colour is the insulation on the earth wire in a UK three-pin plug?
questions.explain: The earth wire is identified by green and yellow striped insulation.

questions.q: Why is the fuse connected in the live wire of a mains appliance?
options: So it disconnects the appliance from the high-voltage supply if too large a current flows
So it increases the current in the circuit
So it stores charge for the appliance
So it lowers the mains frequency
questions.explain: Placed in the live wire, the fuse melts and cuts off the dangerous live supply when the current is too high.

questions.q: How does the resistance of a thermistor change as its temperature increases?
options: Its resistance falls to exactly zero
questions.explain: The resistance of a thermistor decreases as temperature rises, which makes it useful in temperature sensors.

questions.q: How does the resistance of a light-dependent resistor (LDR) change as the light intensity falling on it increases?
questions.explain: An LDR's resistance decreases as light intensity increases, so it is used in light-sensing circuits.

questions.q: What happens when two objects carrying the same type of electric charge are brought close together?
options: There is no force between them
questions.explain: Like charges repel and unlike charges attract.

questions.q: An object becomes positively charged by friction. What has happened to it?
questions.explain: Only electrons move during charging by friction; losing electrons leaves an object with an overall positive charge.

questions.q: In the electric field around an isolated positive charge, which way do the field lines point?
options: There is no field around a stationary charge
questions.explain: Field lines show the direction of force on a positive test charge, so they point away from a positive charge.

questions.q: A 3 ohm resistor and a 6 ohm resistor are connected in series. What is their total resistance?
questions.explain: Resistances in series add together: 3 ohm + 6 ohm = 9 ohm.

questions.q: How does the total resistance of two resistors connected in parallel compare with the individual resistances?
options: It is less than the smaller of the two resistances
It is the sum of the two resistances
It is the average of the two resistances
questions.explain: Adding a resistor in parallel provides an extra path for current, so the total resistance is less than the smallest branch.

questions.q: An appliance operating on the 230 V mains draws a current of 2 A. What is its power?
questions.explain: Using P = VI = 230 V x 2 A = 460 W.
